html:
In the second half of the 8th century Samarkand became the first great papermaking centre of the Islamic world.

Paper had been invented in China; tradition credits Cai Lun in 105 CE. A famous story, told by Arab writers centuries later, says Chinese prisoners taken at the Battle of Talas in 751 taught the craft in Samarkand. Historians now doubt this. Paper was already known along the Silk Road, and the Sogdian Ancient Letters from about 313 were written on it. The craft probably came west through Sogdian trade over a longer time.

Whatever the route, "Samarkand paper", made from linen rags and hemp, became famous. From there the craft spread across the Abbasid Caliphate:

  • a paper mill in Baghdad in the 790s, in the reign of Harun al-Rashid
  • then Damascus, Cairo and North Africa
  • then Muslim Spain, and from there into Christian Europe by the 12th and 13th centuries

Cheap paper replaced papyrus and parchment. It made books, offices and libraries far cheaper, and helped power the scholarship of the Islamic Golden Age.
sum: In the second half of the 8th century Samarkand became the first great papermaking centre of the Islamic world.
